region: Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu

biodiversity_overview.text: 366 GBIF occurrence records for 25 tracked species are attributed to Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, spanning 1996-2026.
363 of these records (99.2%) are located to within 10 km.

species_richness.text: Observed tracked species by group: Aves 19, Mammalia 3, Squamata 1, Magnoliopsida 1, Testudines 1.

threatened_species.text: 3 species with records here are officially threatened (IUCN CR/EN/VU). Names and categories from the IUCN Red List export are not shown in this public snapshot.

notable_species.text: Most recorded species: Indian Cuckoo-shrike (61), Indian Robin (48), White-throated Munia (46), Indian Paradise-flycatcher (33), Indian Golden Oriole (32).

temporal_trends.text: Records per year went from 4 in 2016 to 6 in 2025. This reflects recording effort as much as wildlife and is not a population trend.

protection_coverage.text: Wildlife protected areas (OpenStreetMap national parks, sanctuaries and reserves) cover 2.69% of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu's area (2 areas intersect the state).
6.3% of precisely located records fall inside these areas (23 of 363); this is not a measure of habitat protection.

risk_indicators.text: Highest model-predicted vulnerability among species recorded here (MODEL PREDICTION, not IUCN status): Indian Roofed Turtle (0.36), Indian Thick-knee (0.25), Common Mongoose (0.20), Indian Skimmer (0.19), Mango (0.18).

environmental_pressures.text: Tree cover of at least 30% canopy covered 4 km2 (0.73% of land) in 2000 (Hansen Global Forest Change; includes plantations).

0.0 km2 of that tree cover was lost in 2001-2024 (0.08% of the 2000 extent; 0.0% in 2015-2024, rank 33 of 35 states). The largest annual loss was in 2001 (0.0 km2). Loss includes plantation harvest and natural disturbance; regrowth is not subtracted.
Built-up surfaces cover 3.21% of land and population density is 1,305.9 people per km2 (GHSL 2020).
98% of 30 m tree-cover pixels lie on a forest edge (a fragmentation indicator; higher means more fragmented).
These describe pressures on places; they do not show effects on any species.
